## Proof

Let $K$ be a number field. Denote by $\mathbb{I}_K$ the idèle group, by $|\cdot|:\mathbb{I}_K\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ the idelic norm, and by $\mathbb{I}_K^1=\{x\in\mathbb{I}_K:|x|=1\}$ the norm-one idèles. The diagonal embedding $\iota:K^\times\hookrightarrow\mathbb{I}_K$ lands in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$ by the product formula. We are given that $\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)$ is compact, and we show the ideal class group $\mathrm{Cl}(K)=J_K/P_K$ is finite.

### Step 1. The idèle-to-ideal map

Define $\varphi:\mathbb{I}_K\to J_K$ by
$$\varphi(x)=\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\text{ finite}}\mathfrak{p}^{\,v_{\mathfrak{p}}(x_{\mathfrak{p}})},$$
where $v_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is the normalized valuation. This is well-defined (an idèle has $x_{\mathfrak{p}}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$, hence $v_{\mathfrak{p}}(x_{\mathfrak{p}})=0$, for all but finitely many $\mathfrak{p}$) and is a continuous surjective homomorphism. Surjectivity: given $\mathfrak{a}=\prod\mathfrak{p}^{n_{\mathfrak{p}}}$, pick $x_{\mathfrak{p}}\in K_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ with $v_{\mathfrak{p}}(x_{\mathfrak{p}})=n_{\mathfrak{p}}$ at the finitely many relevant $\mathfrak{p}$, and $x_{\mathfrak{p}}=1$ elsewhere, $x_v=1$ at infinite places.

The kernel is
$$U:=\ker\varphi=\prod_{v\mid\infty}K_v^\times\times\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\text{ finite}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times,$$
the subgroup of idèles that are units at every finite place. Hence $\mathbb{I}_K/U\cong J_K$.

Since $\varphi(\iota(a))=(a)$ for $a\in K^\times$, the image of $\iota(K^\times)$ in $J_K$ is $P_K$ (principal ideals). By the isomorphism theorem:
$$\mathrm{Cl}(K)=J_K/P_K\cong \mathbb{I}_K\big/\bigl(U\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr).\tag{1}$$

### Step 2. Reduction to the norm-one subgroup

Set $U^1:=U\cap\mathbb{I}_K^1=\{x\in U:\prod_{v\mid\infty}|x_v|_v=1\}$. We claim
$$\mathrm{Cl}(K)\cong \mathbb{I}_K^1\big/\bigl(U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr).\tag{2}$$

The norm map restricted to $U$ surjects onto $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$: for any $t>0$, choose an infinite place $v_0$ and $u_{v_0}\in K_{v_0}^\times$ with $|u_{v_0}|_{v_0}=t$ (at a real place take $u_{v_0}=t$; at a complex place take $u_{v_0}=\sqrt{t}$), setting $u_v=1$ at other infinite places and $u_{\mathfrak{p}}=1$ at finite places. Then $|u|=t$. Since $|\iota(a)|=1$ for $a\in K^\times$, the subgroup $U\cdot\iota(K^\times)$ surjects onto $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ under $|\cdot|$.

As $\mathbb{I}_K^1=\ker|\cdot|$, this gives $\mathbb{I}_K=\mathbb{I}_K^1\cdot U\cdot\iota(K^\times)$. Therefore
$$\mathbb{I}_K\big/\bigl(U\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr)\cong\mathbb{I}_K^1\big/\bigl(\mathbb{I}_K^1\cap U\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr).$$
If $x\in\mathbb{I}_K^1\cap U\cdot\iota(K^\times)$, write $x=u\cdot\iota(a)$ with $u\in U$, $a\in K^\times$; then $1=|x|=|u|\cdot|\iota(a)|=|u|$, so $u\in U^1$, giving $x\in U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Hence $\mathbb{I}_K^1\cap U\cdot\iota(K^\times)=U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)$, proving (2).

### Step 3. Compactness of $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$

From (2),
$$\mathrm{Cl}(K)\cong\bigl(\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)\bigr)\big/\bigl(U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)/\iota(K^\times)\bigr).$$
The quotient map $q:\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)\to\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ is continuous and surjective. Since $\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)$ is compact (given), its continuous image $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ is **compact**.

### Step 4. Discreteness of $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$

The subgroup $U^1=U\cap\mathbb{I}_K^1$ is **open** in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$: at each finite place $\mathfrak{p}$, the condition $x_{\mathfrak{p}}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ is open (since $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ is open in $K_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$), and these are restricted-product conditions. Hence $U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)=\bigcup_{a\in K^\times}\iota(a)\cdot U^1$ is open in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$.

Therefore every coset of $U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)$ in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$ is open, so the quotient $\mathbb{I}_K^1/(U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times))\cong\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ carries the **discrete** topology.

### Step 5. Conclusion

$\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ is simultaneously compact (Step 3) and discrete (Step 4). A discrete compact space is finite: the open cover $\{\{[x]\}:x\in\mathbb{I}_K^1\}$ by singletons admits a finite subcover by compactness, so only finitely many cosets exist. Hence
$$h_K:=|\mathrm{Cl}(K)|<\infty.$$

Denote by $\mathbb{I}_K$ the idèle group, by $|\cdot|:\mathbb{I}_K\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ the idelic norm, and by $\mathbb{I}_K^1=\{x\in\mathbb{I}_K:|x|=1\}$ the norm-one idèles. The diagonal embedding $\iota:K^\times\hookrightarrow\mathbb{I}_K$ lands in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$ by the product formula. We are given that $\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)$ is compact, and we show the ideal class group $\mathrm{Cl}(K)=J_K/P_K$ is finite.

### Step 1. The idèle-to-ideal map

Define $\varphi:\mathbb{I}_K\to J_K$ by
$$\varphi(x)=\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\text{ finite}}\mathfrak{p}^{\,v_{\mathfrak{p}}(x_{\mathfrak{p}})},$$
where $v_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is the normalized valuation. This is well-defined (an idèle has $x_{\mathfrak{p}}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$, hence $v_{\mathfrak{p}}(x_{\mathfrak{p}})=0$, for all but finitely many $\mathfrak{p}$) and is a continuous surjective homomorphism. Surjectivity: given $\mathfrak{a}=\prod\mathfrak{p}^{n_{\mathfrak{p}}}$, pick $x_{\mathfrak{p}}\in K_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ with $v_{\mathfrak{p}}(x_{\mathfrak{p}})=n_{\mathfrak{p}}$ at the finitely many relevant $\mathfrak{p}$, and $x_{\mathfrak{p}}=1$ elsewhere, $x_v=1$ at infinite places.

The kernel is
$$U:=\ker\varphi=\prod_{v\mid\infty}K_v^\times\times\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\text{ finite}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times,$$
the subgroup of idèles that are units at every finite place. Hence $\mathbb{I}_K/U\cong J_K$.

Since $\varphi(\iota(a))=(a)$ for $a\in K^\times$, the image of $\iota(K^\times)$ in $J_K$ is $P_K$ (principal ideals). By the isomorphism theorem:
$$\mathrm{Cl}(K)=J_K/P_K\cong \mathbb{I}_K\big/\bigl(U\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr).\tag{1}$$

### Step 2. Reduction to the norm-one subgroup

Set $U^1:=U\cap\mathbb{I}_K^1=\{x\in U:\prod_{v\mid\infty}|x_v|_v=1\}$. We claim
$$\mathrm{Cl}(K)\cong \mathbb{I}_K^1\big/\bigl(U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr).\tag{2}$$

The norm map restricted to $U$ surjects onto $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$: for any $t>0$, choose an infinite place $v_0$ and $u_{v_0}\in K_{v_0}^\times$ with $|u_{v_0}|_{v_0}=t$ (at a real place take $u_{v_0}=t$; at a complex place take $u_{v_0}=\sqrt{t}$), setting $u_v=1$ at other infinite places and $u_{\mathfrak{p}}=1$ at finite places. Then $|u|=t$. Since $|\iota(a)|=1$ for $a\in K^\times$, the subgroup $U\cdot\iota(K^\times)$ surjects onto $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ under $|\cdot|$.

As $\mathbb{I}_K^1=\ker|\cdot|$, this gives $\mathbb{I}_K=\mathbb{I}_K^1\cdot U\cdot\iota(K^\times)$. Therefore
$$\mathbb{I}_K\big/\bigl(U\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr)\cong\mathbb{I}_K^1\big/\bigl(\mathbb{I}_K^1\cap U\cdot\iota(K^\times)\bigr).$$
If $x\in\mathbb{I}_K^1\cap U\cdot\iota(K^\times)$, write $x=u\cdot\iota(a)$ with $u\in U$, $a\in K^\times$; then $1=|x|=|u|\cdot|\iota(a)|=|u|$, so $u\in U^1$, giving $x\in U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Hence $\mathbb{I}_K^1\cap U\cdot\iota(K^\times)=U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)$, proving (2).

### Step 3. Compactness of $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$

From (2),
$$\mathrm{Cl}(K)\cong\bigl(\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)\bigr)\big/\bigl(U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)/\iota(K^\times)\bigr).$$
The quotient map $q:\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)\to\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ is continuous and surjective. Since $\mathbb{I}_K^1/\iota(K^\times)$ is compact (given), its continuous image $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ is **compact**.

### Step 4. Discreteness of $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$

The subgroup $U^1=U\cap\mathbb{I}_K^1$ is **open** in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$: at each finite place $\mathfrak{p}$, the condition $x_{\mathfrak{p}}\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ is open (since $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ is open in $K_{\mathfrak{p}}^\times$), and these are restricted-product conditions. Hence $U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)=\bigcup_{a\in K^\times}\iota(a)\cdot U^1$ is open in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$.

Therefore every coset of $U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times)$ in $\mathbb{I}_K^1$ is open, so the quotient $\mathbb{I}_K^1/(U^1\cdot\iota(K^\times))\cong\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ carries the **discrete** topology.

### Step 5. Conclusion

$\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ is simultaneously compact (Step 3) and discrete (Step 4). A discrete compact space is finite: the open cover $\{\{[x]\}:x\in\mathbb{I}_K^1\}$ by singletons admits a finite subcover by compactness, so only finitely many cosets exist. Hence
$$h_K:=|\mathrm{Cl}(K)|<\infty.$$
